properties.name: A thing done wrong is CORRECTED at its root, never patched around — and before 1.0, compatibility is not a reason to defer the correction
properties.statement:
TWO CLAUSES, AND THEY HAVE DIFFERENT LIFESPANS. The first draft of this rule ran them together and said the whole thing should be revisited at 1.0; Anthony corrected that on 2026-08-17 — he wants the philosophy ENDURING. Separating them is what makes that possible, because only one of them is about version numbers.

⭐ CLAUSE 1 — THE PHILOSOPHY. IT NEVER EXPIRES.
When something is wrong, go back to the drawing board, work out how it should have been done, and re-implement it properly. A workaround, a shim, or a repair that leaves the original mistake in place is not a fix; it is a decision to carry the mistake and pay interest on it. This is a claim about how to build, not about when — it is as true at 1.0 and at 10.0 as it is today.

ANTHONY, 2026-08-17, asking for it to be made permanent: "I'm not sure how many fixes have been patches versus going back to the drawing board, planning how it should have been done correctly, and then re-implementing proper fix, but I'd like to start now. this is my philosophy on how to build something - so ensuring that it is built into the design of reflow2."

CLAUSE 2 — THE PRE-1.0 COROLLARY. THIS ONE DOES CHANGE AT 1.0.
"It would break consumers" is not, on its own, a reason to keep a defect — it is a reason to correct it NOW rather than later. THE COST ARGUMENT RUNS OPPOSITE TO THE INSTINCT: the instinct is that a break is expensive so defer it; the instinct has the price right and the TREND backwards. The price of a break rises with every consumer, so deferring buys the same change later at a higher cost, in a worse currency — user trust, migration effort, and fear of touching code that works.

His words, 2026-08-17: "I'd rather pay for this change now than when we have hundreds/thousands of users and we can't make big changes out of fear that we may upset something that is working."

CHANGELOG.md already says 1.0 is "deferred until a stability commitment — the design surface promising compatibility". Clause 2 is the other side of that sentence: until the commitment exists the surface is explicitly not promising, and behaving as though it were is itself the mistake. WHEN THAT COMMITMENT IS MADE, CLAUSE 2 IS REPLACED BY A DEPRECATION DISCIPLINE — not dropped. Clause 1 is untouched by it: after 1.0 the correct fix still gets designed properly; it ships behind a deprecation window instead of immediately.

⚠️ AND MEASURE THE COST BEFORE LETTING IT DECIDE. This is the lesson the rule was born from rather than an aside. `dec:a-misnaming-is-fixed-in-the-message-not-the-key` declined a rename because it would "break every consumer" — asserted, never measured. Measured afterwards: 14 code files, 6 live docs, and PERSISTED AS DATA NOWHERE, so the migration being protected against did not exist. An unmeasured cost is the easiest way to talk yourself out of the right fix, and it is invisible when it works, because nothing happens.

WHAT IT IS NOT. Not licence to rewrite what merely displeases — the trigger is something WRONG, not something one would style differently. Not licence to widen a task under cover of another. And not licence for an agent to settle intent: `rule:design-intent-moves-only-on-the-owners-word` is untouched.

ENFORCEMENT: ADVISORY, on Anthony's word 2026-08-17, asked as "if a session shipped a workaround instead of the full fix — tests green, change reviewed — should the build have stopped them?" He said advice. That is also the honest answer mechanically: whether the full fix was taken is a JUDGEMENT about intent, not a fact about graph state, so an enforced flag here would owe a detector that cannot be written. WHAT CAN BE MECHANIZED IS THE ADJACENT THING — not judging the fix, but making the CLAIM recordable and countable, which is `req:a-fix-says-whether-it-corrected-the-cause`. The rule states the philosophy; the requirement gives it somewhere to live.
